summary: The Spring calculator works out spring index from the spring constant (k), the modulus of rigidity, the free length for plain ends and number of active coils (Na). Think of it as a shortcut for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Spring calculator work?
sections.html:
The Spring calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports spring index in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (select your spring purpose and the choice spring end); then you type in the spring constant (k) (Traction compression spring), the modulus of rigidity (G), the free length for plain ends and number of active coils (Na) (Spring design results).

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Spring calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Extension/compression Δx=-force applied to the spring (F) ÷ spring constant (k)
Mean diameter (D)=(1 ÷ 2) × (modulus of rigidity (G) × (wire diameter (d) ^ 4) ÷ (number of active coils (Na) × spring constant (k)))
Spring index (C)=(outer diameter (OD) − wire diameter (d)) ÷ wire diameter (d)
Mean diameter (D)=spring index (C) × wire diameter (d)
Mean diameter (D)=outer diameter (OD) − wire diameter (d)
Pitch=(free length for plain ends − wire diameter (d)) ÷ number of active coils (Na)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Force, opening in newtons
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Force per length, opening in newtons per meter
  • Pressure, opening in gigapascals
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Spring calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the spring constant (k), the modulus of rigidity and the free length for plain ends — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Spring calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns spring index, derived from the spring constant (k), the modulus of rigidity and the free length for plain ends. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Spring calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the spring constant (k), the modulus of rigidity, the free length for plain ends and number of active coils (Na), which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter outer diameter (OD) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Outer diameter (OD) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Spring calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
